items.title: See
items.text: Visit a cultural centre, library or heritage museum. Article 35 of the law asks them to show heritage

items.title: Ask
items.text: Ask who the bearer of an item is, and whether they still practise it

items.title: Check
items.text: Look up a claimed bearer in the national list on the China ICH website, and report fake livestreams

items.title: Record
items.text: With your elders' consent, record family customs, dialect and skills, noting who, where and when

items.title: Learn
items.text: If you want to learn a craft, plan in years, not a single taster class

footnote: These are suggestions, and none of them guarantees anything. Basis: ICH Law, Articles 14, 20 and 35
notes: Five things to take home. They are suggestions, and none of them guarantees an outcome, but all of them are within reach. See: go to your local cultural centre, library or heritage museum. Article 35 of the law asks public cultural institutions to show and explain heritage, and tonight's talk is part of that. Ask: when you watch a performance or a demonstration, ask who the bearer is and whether they still practise it. Check: if someone calls themselves a bearer or calls a product heritage, you can look up the item and region in the national list on the China ICH website. If they do not match, buy it as an ordinary product and do not pay extra for the label. If you see a livestream misusing the official heritage logo or claiming cures, you can complain to the market regulator. Record: with your elders' consent, record your family's festival customs, dialect and skills, and write down who, where and when. Article 14 of the law allows citizens to carry out heritage surveys. Learn: if you really want to learn a craft, plan in years, not a single taster class. Also, Cultural and Natural Heritage Day falls on the second Saturday of June. And if you think something near you deserves a place on the list, Article 20 lets you propose it to the provincial culture department.
